Title: Bank results reveal stark divide as industry recovers from turmoil
Text: [Profits for JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Wells Fargo (WFC) surged in the second quarter while falling sharply at Citigroup (C), demonstrating a divide in how the banking world is faring as it recovers from a period of extreme turmoil.JPMorgan and Wells Fargo showed that some giants can continue to make lots of money from consumer loans even as industry deposit costs rise while leaning on their sprawling franchises to generate additional revenue.What Citigroup revealed is that a number of problems continue to plague even the biggest institutions, especially those that rely heavily on dealmaking and trading.Citigroup's profit tumbled 36% in the second quarter, largely because of weaknesses in its Wall Street unit.Other banks reporting next week, such as Goldman Sachs (GS) and Morgan Stanley (MS), could run into similar challenges."The long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize, making for a disappointing quarter," said Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser.JPMorgan and Wells were essentially flat in Friday trading, while the stock of Citigroup closed down 4%.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)A warning for smaller banksThere was also a new warning Friday for smaller banks. That came from State Street (STT), which was the nation's 12th largest as of March 31.In its second quarter results, State Street disclosed that its net interest income, which measures the difference between what it earns from loans and pays out in deposits, fell 10% when compared to the first quarter.That's largely because of rising deposit rates and a rotation by customers out of non-interest-bearing deposits as they seek higher yields. The bank now expects net interest income to drop 12% to 18% in the coming quarter.Read more: High-yield savings account vs. CD: Which is right for you?"What we found is that our larger clients, and we primarily have large, sophisticated clients, are quite active in thinking about their alternatives, and... that has been accelerated by the swiftness of this cycle and the place that we've come to and the speed," said Eric Aboaf, State Street CFO.Story continuesSome other mid-sized banks that report their results in the coming weeks have already revised down their expectations for how much of this income they can earn, including executives for US Bancorp (USB), Citizens Financial Group (CFG), Comerica (CMA), Huntington (HBAN), KeyCorp (KEY), and Zions (ZION).State Street's stock closed down 12% Friday.Navigating the chaosThe results kicked off a closely watched earnings season where banks of all sizes will be trying to show that they recovered from one of the most tumultuous periods for the industry since the 2008 financial crisis.JPMorgan demonstrated its hold over the rest of the industry during the chaos of the spring by winning a government-run auction to purchase the bulk of operations of First Republic after regulators seized the San Francisco lender.First Republic was one of three sizable regional banks to fail, along with Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. Their seizures triggered a panic in the banking system and outflows of depositors from a number of smaller banks.The deal lifted JPMorgan's second quarter numbers. It said First Republic added $2.4 billion to net income. That helped push overall earnings to $14.5 billion, up 67% from the same period a year ago. Wells Fargo's earnings of $4.9 billion were up 57%.Trouble on Wall StreetThe industry is no longer at the same crisis level as it was in the spring, but second quarter results from some of the biggest banks contained reminders that the industry still faces a number of challenges on several fronts.Citigroup, for example, struggled with a recent drought of dealmaking that is making day-to-day life more difficult for all of Wall Street. Its investment banking revenues fell by 24% to $612 million. Trading was another weakness. Revenue from that activity fell 13%.Citigroup and other firms with big investment banking and trading units have made or announced cuts of roughly 12,000 jobs since the end of 2022. Dealmaking is drying up amid a rise in interest rates and economic uncertainty.Even JPMorgan had challenges on this front. Its investment banking fees fell by 6% from a year ago to $1.5 billion. Its trading revenues from equities and fixed income also fell.'Things are better than people would have expected'What JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup had in common Friday is that they set aside more money to cover future loan losses, a sign they expect the economy to slow in the coming quarters.Many other banks are also expected to do the same when they report their second quarter results.Wells Fargo set aside $1.71 billion in provisions for credit losses in the second quarter, compared with $580 million a year ago. That included a $949 million increase primarily for commercial real estate office loans."I think things are better than people would have expected at this point in the cycle," said Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo. "We do expect that they'll be more weakness in the [commercial real estate] market and it's going to take a while to play out. It'll be a while before we see you know, the end of end of this."CEO Charlie Scharf said the US economy "continues to be resilient."JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon. REUTERS/Brian Snyder (Brian Snyder / reuters)JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon also sounded optimistic about the US economy, saying it "continues to be resilient" and that "consumers are spending, albeit a little more slowly."His CFO, Jeremy Barnum, told reporters the bank does not expect a lot of loan demand except for credit cards and autos. But "we don't particularly expect to be tightening other than to the extent that individual borrow credit metrics deteriorate."Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: Wall Street says the worst is over for Wall Street
Text: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. So far investors agree.Top bank executives spent much of this past week pointing to "green shoots" in dealmaking or trading despite in most cases logging another disappointing quarter.Morgan Stanley (MS) CFO Sharon Yeshaya said that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."Citigroup (C) CFO Mark Mason said "we are seeing green shoots" in the issuance of debt "as clients start to have a greater conviction" about the direction of interest rates.Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon said Wednesday that the month of June "was certainly better" than the earlier part of the quarter and that he has noticed more "risk-on sentiment" in July.David M. Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs. (REUTERS/Mike Blake) (Mike Blake / reuters)"It definitely feels better over the course of the last six to eight weeks than it felt earlier in the year."That's certainly what investors wanted to hear. Stocks of most big banks rose this past week. Morgan Stanley's stock was up more than 6% on Tuesday after its results were released. Goldman's stock even rose more than 1% Wednesday despite reporting that profits fell by 58%, more than expected.Yet the performance of Wall Street's core businesses were certainly nothing to celebrate across most banks. Trading revenue fell by 22% at Morgan Stanley, 14% at Goldman, 13% at Citigroup, and 10% at JPMorgan Chase. Only Bank of America (BAC) had trading revenue rise, by 7%.The drops were not as much as analysts expected at all but one firm, Morgan Stanley.Investment banking revenues were down by 24% at Citi, 20% at Goldman, and 6% at JPMorgan. They were flat at Morgan Stanley and up 1.6% at Bank of America.The drops at Goldman and Citigroup were worse than expected. For the others, the results beat estimates.'We feel good about where we are'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Story continuesGoldman, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup were among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 20,000 jobs since the end of 2022, resulting in hundreds of millions in severance costs.Goldman spent $260 million through the first half of the year and Citigroup spent $450 million. Morgan Stanley's severance costs were $308 million in the second quarter.Some executives hinted this week that the headcount reductions were likely over."I'm glad we were early in January to work on head count sizing," Solomon said, referring to a decision that month to lay off more than 3,000 workers. But now, "we feel good about where we are."'We will see'Solomon said he is noticing activity picking up in a few spots, citing equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so and then they start to improve," the CEO said. "And so I think we're starting to see that here. It definitely feels better."Goldman, he added, doesn't have to go back to the boom period of 2021 to see "material uplift."At Morgan Stanley, Yeshaya said the firm's backlog of deals is on the rise and M&A activity is picking up in energy and financials.Mason, at Citigoup, cited a "healthy" M&A pipeline "which we would expect to unlock as the sentiment continues to improve." Still the company has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A.His boss, CEO Jane Fraser, also sounded a cautious note. In a release she said that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."Then she told analysts "corporates are pretty cautious," citing the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, tensions with China, and concerns about limited economic growth.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)"I think clients have been trying to understand and get their arms around both the macro and the market outlook for a while," she added. "I think they now seem to accept the current environment is the new normal and are beginning to position themselves globally."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. Text: [In this article, we discuss 12 highest yielding Dow Jones dividend stocks. (NYSE:VZ), Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc. (NASDAQ:WBA), and 3M Company (NYSE:MMM) among others that are mentioned below.Story continues12 Highest Yielding Dow Jones Dividend StocksOur Methodology:For this article, we examined the companies within the Dow Jones index and identified 12 stocks with the highest dividend yields as of July 19. Text: [Carvana shares close higher after announcing a deal to trim its debt by over $1.2 billion. They've had a lot of troubles with their wine business. Their beer business-- Corona, Modelo have been on fire. And most notably, and I have a story on the Yahoo Finance home page now, that business Corona Light has picked up market share because of everything going on with Bud Light. So I see what Elliott's talking-- Elliott's talking about here.SEAN SMITH: Yeah, exactly. And I think when analysts look at this name even when they look at one of the competitors out there like a Molson Coors who has been able to chip away at that market share that Bud Light has lost within the beer category, whether or not those new customers, drinkers are going to stick with their brands, or if they're going to trade back to Bud Light.And it almost seems like the line of thinking here from analysts is that they think that a name like Constellation Brands is going to be able to hold on to those new customers because people don't seem to be going back to Bud Light the rate that we had initially or the Street had initially expected here when we did see that--- And I want to publicly thank you, Sean Smith, because you were the one that told me to put lime in my Bud--SEAN SMITH: Lemon.- Lemon--SEAN SMITH: --the Bud Light--- And it's good. I encourage you to give it a try. Maybe while looking at these awful results from Goldman.SEAN SMITH: That was my college drink, and I still, to this day, here and there-- well, try it. Title: These Stocks Are Moving the Most Today: Carvana, AT&T, Goldman, Northern Trust, Joby, and More
Goldman Sachs earnings: 'The bad news is out,' analyst says
Text: [Goldman Sachs shares are on the rise despite reporting a Q2 profit miss. Wells Fargo Managing Director Mike Mayo sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to detail his outlook on Goldman Sachs as the banking institution pivots away from consumer services and CEO David Solomon's vision comes into question. Mayo shares his opinion on banking leadership succession plans while stating Goldman Sachs may have had its "second-worst quarter" under Solomon's helm, while excluding the pandemic years.Video Transcript- Goldman Sachs rounding out second quarter earnings season from the big banks and, well, it wasn't pretty. Profits tanked 58%, hit by write downs in the company's consumer and asset management businesses. Embattled CEO, David Solomon, told investors on the conference call, he is confident in his strategy. But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

Title: UPDATE 1-Goldman brings back Tom Montag as CEO Solomon bolsters board support
Text: [(Adds CEO comment in paragraph 8)July 20 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs has brought back to its fold senior executive Tom Montag, adding him to its board as the Wall Street giant looks to regain lost ground after its ill-fated foray into consumer banking.Montag, who had previously co-headed Goldman's securities division and held other senior roles in his 22 years at the firm, will join the audit, governance and risk committees.Considered to be an ally of CEO David Solomon, Montag could bolster support for the chief executive, who is looking to undo the damage from the company's high-profile flop in retail banking.Solomon's plans to refocus Goldman to its mainstay businesses of investment banking, trading and asset management is already gaining traction with the board, two sources close to the CEO told Reuters."Tom has deep risk acumen that will further strengthen the depth and breadth of skills and experiences represented on our Board," said Adebayo Ogunlesi, the bank's lead director.Montag left Goldman to join Merrill Lynch in 2008, which was then taken over by Bank of America during the throes of the financial crisis.He also served as BofA's chief operating officer and the president of its global banking and markets division before retiring at the end of 2021. Last year, he became CEO of Rubicon Carbon, a TPG-backed firm working on developing carbon markets."Tom brings extensive financial services and risk management experience, with over 35 years in the industry," Solomon said. "He has incredible perspective regarding the complex financial and non-financial risks that large global financial institutions face."Goldman had on Wednesday reported its lowest quarterly profit in three years, hit by writedowns tied to its consumer businesses and real estate investments."This moment in the economic cycle creates meaningful headwinds for Goldman Sachs... We are making tough decisions that are driving the strategic evolution of the firm," Solomon told analysts, warning that the bank was heading into "a period of lower results."(Reporting by Saeed Azhar in New York and Niket Nishant and Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Arun Koyyur and Lananh Nguyen)]

Text: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. So far investors agree.Top bank executives spent much of this past week pointing to "green shoots" in dealmaking or trading despite in most cases logging another disappointing quarter.Morgan Stanley (MS) CFO Sharon Yeshaya said that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."Citigroup (C) CFO Mark Mason said "we are seeing green shoots" in the issuance of debt "as clients start to have a greater conviction" about the direction of interest rates.Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon said Wednesday that the month of June "was certainly better" than the earlier part of the quarter and that he has noticed more "risk-on sentiment" in July.David M. Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs. (REUTERS/Mike Blake) (Mike Blake / reuters)"It definitely feels better over the course of the last six to eight weeks than it felt earlier in the year."That's certainly what investors wanted to hear. Stocks of most big banks rose this past week. Morgan Stanley's stock was up more than 6% on Tuesday after its results were released. Goldman's stock even rose more than 1% Wednesday despite reporting that profits fell by 58%, more than expected.Yet the performance of Wall Street's core businesses were certainly nothing to celebrate across most banks. Trading revenue fell by 22% at Morgan Stanley, 14% at Goldman, 13% at Citigroup, and 10% at JPMorgan Chase. Only Bank of America (BAC) had trading revenue rise, by 7%.The drops were not as much as analysts expected at all but one firm, Morgan Stanley.Investment banking revenues were down by 24% at Citi, 20% at Goldman, and 6% at JPMorgan. They were flat at Morgan Stanley and up 1.6% at Bank of America.The drops at Goldman and Citigroup were worse than expected. For the others, the results beat estimates.'We feel good about where we are'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Story continuesGoldman, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup were among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 20,000 jobs since the end of 2022, resulting in hundreds of millions in severance costs.Goldman spent $260 million through the first half of the year and Citigroup spent $450 million. Morgan Stanley's severance costs were $308 million in the second quarter.Some executives hinted this week that the headcount reductions were likely over."I'm glad we were early in January to work on head count sizing," Solomon said, referring to a decision that month to lay off more than 3,000 workers. But now, "we feel good about where we are."'We will see'Solomon said he is noticing activity picking up in a few spots, citing equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so and then they start to improve," the CEO said. "And so I think we're starting to see that here. It definitely feels better."Goldman, he added, doesn't have to go back to the boom period of 2021 to see "material uplift."At Morgan Stanley, Yeshaya said the firm's backlog of deals is on the rise and M&A activity is picking up in energy and financials.Mason, at Citigoup, cited a "healthy" M&A pipeline "which we would expect to unlock as the sentiment continues to improve." Still the company has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A.His boss, CEO Jane Fraser, also sounded a cautious note. In a release she said that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."Then she told analysts "corporates are pretty cautious," citing the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, tensions with China, and concerns about limited economic growth.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)"I think clients have been trying to understand and get their arms around both the macro and the market outlook for a while," she added. "I think they now seem to accept the current environment is the new normal and are beginning to position themselves globally."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: UPDATE 1-Goldman brings back Tom Montag as CEO Solomon bolsters board support
Text: [(Adds CEO comment in paragraph 8)July 20 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs has brought back to its fold senior executive Tom Montag, adding him to its board as the Wall Street giant looks to regain lost ground after its ill-fated foray into consumer banking.Montag, who had previously co-headed Goldman's securities division and held other senior roles in his 22 years at the firm, will join the audit, governance and risk committees.Considered to be an ally of CEO David Solomon, Montag could bolster support for the chief executive, who is looking to undo the damage from the company's high-profile flop in retail banking.Solomon's plans to refocus Goldman to its mainstay businesses of investment banking, trading and asset management is already gaining traction with the board, two sources close to the CEO told Reuters."Tom has deep risk acumen that will further strengthen the depth and breadth of skills and experiences represented on our Board," said Adebayo Ogunlesi, the bank's lead director.Montag left Goldman to join Merrill Lynch in 2008, which was then taken over by Bank of America during the throes of the financial crisis.He also served as BofA's chief operating officer and the president of its global banking and markets division before retiring at the end of 2021. Last year, he became CEO of Rubicon Carbon, a TPG-backed firm working on developing carbon markets."Tom brings extensive financial services and risk management experience, with over 35 years in the industry," Solomon said. "He has incredible perspective regarding the complex financial and non-financial risks that large global financial institutions face."Goldman had on Wednesday reported its lowest quarterly profit in three years, hit by writedowns tied to its consumer businesses and real estate investments."This moment in the economic cycle creates meaningful headwinds for Goldman Sachs... We are making tough decisions that are driving the strategic evolution of the firm," Solomon told analysts, warning that the bank was heading into "a period of lower results."(Reporting by Saeed Azhar in New York and Niket Nishant and Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Arun Koyyur and Lananh Nguyen)]

Fed set to propose new banking capital requirements, 'Basel III endgame'
Text: [Fed officials are set to unveil an overhaul of banking capital requirements, known as the "Basel III endgame," this week. American Banker Staff Writer Kyle Campbell sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to explain the ways in which these guidelines will mitigate risk differently for various forms of credit lending. Campbell describes how these new guidelines will impact certain larger, institutional banks, while examining the exposure regional banks may have to commercial real estate.Video Transcript- All right. On Thursday, just one day after the FOMC's latest interest rate decision, Federal Reserve will unveil a proposal for new bank capital requirements. The proposed rule would also lower the threshold for qualifying banks, meaning smaller institutions will face a new host of demands previously avoided.Fed vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr, outlined a sweeping plan to overhaul bank oversight requirements earlier this month. The proposal, set to come out Thursday, will offer more specifics on just how significant those changes could be.Joining us now with the latest is Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker. Kyle, good to see you here. I talked to Brian Moynihan, CEO of Bank of America, about this. He really took a-- I would say, a hard line view of this. This could really be impactful to the economy. What have you been hearing from sources?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, I mean, that's the big concern, right. Banks have been looking forward to this proposal for a long time now. Since 2017 is when the Basel III, they call it endgame, was first finalized, sort of, internationally, and now we're implementing that.Where this is-- what we're going to see on Thursday is just how that's going to impact the economy because we're going to find out which particular activities are going to be given which sort of risk weights under the new framework. So if, let's say, auto lending comes with a much heavier capital penalty, than a lot of banks are sort of forecasting with their internal models currently. It's going to make that type of financing more expensive, essentially.Story continuesAnd there is a view that as capital overall increases, it's just going to have a broader, sort of, tightening impact on the availability of credit broadly in the economy.- Is it really? Or is it just that their margins are going to get smaller? Or both, right?KYLE CAMPBELL: I think it's probably a bit of both but that's a great question. And certainly, consumer advocates are saying, well, look, the way that capital is raised is it's just hurting the bottom line for executives. You just have to retained earnings and you lose that sort of ROE, return on equity, that is what sort of fuels bank profits.So it's certainly going to result in less profitability, at least for some period of time. And again, how that actually impacts the availability of credit to the average person is going to really, I think-- I don't think it's particularly useful to try to forecast the overall picture, but you can get a good sense of how individual banks are going to be impacted by this once we see the specifics on Thursday.- For those banks, let's say a Wells Fargo, that have been struggling for some time, what does this mean for the struggling banks like a Wells Fargo?KYLE CAMPBELL: Wells Fargo, it'll be interesting. I mean, obviously if-- I mean, they've started to sort of move away from mortgages, which is one area where there's going to be a lot of focus. What happens to mortgages. You know, how does it get treated under the capital rules.I mean-- I think that where it's going to be more impactful than at Wells Fargo-- I mean, certainly they're going to be hit to some degree. But I think it's really going to be most impactful on the sort of mid-size banks, if you will. The ones that were in that sort of 100 billion to 250 billion asset range, that are now going to be facing these capital-- these sort of risk capital requirements for the first time.I think the large banks sort of know how to deal with these sort of requirements. And I don't think that a Wells Fargo is going to be as impacted, on a relative basis, as some of the smaller banks.- Let's turn to another issue that the market's been paying a lot of attention to, and that's commercial real estate and the risks associated with commercial real estate. In these earnings reports that we've gotten from banks, several of them announced steps to anticipate losses. To put aside money for losses, potential losses in commercial real estate.Wells Fargo, for example, boosted its allowance for credit losses. So where are we in that sort of situation?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, that's a great question. And certainly, regulators are very focused on commercial real estate, giving some strong warnings to banks to do things like set aside losses and sort of avoid getting new exposures where you can avoid it.And that actually kind of compounds the issue because a lot of these-- I mean, certainly with offices, we know, the ones that are vacant, not getting people in, and that's sort of a whole issue unto itself. Title: PacWest is helping regulators make their case for bolstering US banks
Text: [A regional lender in Beverly Hills may have helped regulators bolster the case they plan to make Thursday to shore up banks across the US.PacWest (PACW), which had been struggling to recover from the downfall of Silicon Valley Bank in March, on Tuesday said it found a rescuer in Banc of California (BANC). The two plan to combine with $400 million in financing from private equity firms Warburg Pincus and Centerbridge.The announcement was a fresh reminder that the turmoil that started in the spring is still not over for the banking industry, which still faces questions about its strength as lenders struggle with high interest rates, rising funding costs, and declining profitability.PacWest stock declined 27% Tuesday and then soared 27% Wednesday.The deal is "a reminder that the stresses on the banking system aren’t all just bad management at one firm," MacroPolicy Perspectives founder Julia Coronado told Yahoo Finance Wednesday. "It is the inverted yield curve, it’s a generational shock in interest rates that banks are having to grapple with ... and that’s a reality that makes it hard for banks to make money."The fresh volatility may come in handy for regulators as the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency try to sell a complex overhaul of new capital standards for banks on Thursday.They argue the changes are needed to make lenders stronger, more resilient, and better prepared for shocks like the crisis of this spring, when the failures of Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, and First Republic triggered deposit withdrawals across the banking world. PacWest, caught up in that panic, sold assets to bolster its liquidity and capital strength.The new capital proposals are expected to face pushback from the banking industry, which argues that lenders are much more resilient than they were during the 2008-09 financial crisis and that higher requirements could restrict lending.Story continuesRead more: How to get a personal loan with bad creditFederal Reserve's vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr. (Andrew Harnik/AP Photo) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr said earlier this month that the Fed would principally raise capital requirements for the largest, most complex banks. The biggest institutions will be asked to hold an additional 2 percentage points of capital — or an additional $2 of capital for every $100 of risk-weighted assets. Capital is the buffer banks have to hold to absorb future losses.He also said regulators would widen the scope of the new rules to institutions with as few as $100 billion in assets, meaning roughly 30 banks would be subject to them. The combined PacWest and Banc of California would be under that cap, based on their combined assets of $36 billion.'Risk weights'These changes are part of the US version of an international accord known as Basel III that was developed following the 2008 crisis by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.The goal of that committee — which was convened by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland — was to set global regulatory capital standards so that banks would have enough in reserve to survive crises. The last version of this accord was agreed to in 2017, but plans to roll it out in the US were delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.A key component of the revised rules will be a series of so-called "risk weights" applied to various assets banks hold. The riskier the assets are, the more capital banks will be required to set aside to absorb any future losses. Those assets can range from Treasuries and mortgages to derivatives and cryptocurrencies.Read more: CDs vs. bonds: Which is right for me?Barr has said that most banks already have enough capital to meet the new standards and estimated that banks would be able to build the required capital through retained earnings in less than two years — even while maintaining their dividends."These changes would increase capital requirements overall, but I want to emphasize that they would principally raise capital requirements for the largest, most complex banks," he said in a speech earlier this month at the Bipartisan Policy Center in Washington.He also made it clear that banks would have time to weigh in with any comments before the proposal is final. "We intend to consider comments carefully and any changes would be implemented with an appropriate phase-in," he said, adding that most banks already have enough capital to meet the new requirements.Betsy Graseck, an equity analyst for Morgan Stanley, said she anticipates the "phase-in" for the largest banks to take three to five years."A later phase in would be a positive for the group as it enables additional capital accretion through earnings generation," Graseck wrote in a Tuesday research note. "An earlier, or shorter, phase in would be a negative."By Graseck’s calculations, JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC) can cover the increased capital requirements from earnings in less than two years’ time. It would take Goldman Sachs (GS) three years and Citigroup (C) four years, she said.'Dancing in the streets'Banks are expected to push back."Further capital requirements on the largest US banks will lead to higher borrowing costs and fewer loans for consumers and businesses — slowing our economy and impacting those on the margin hardest," Kevin Fromer, chief executive of bank lobbying group the Financial Services Forum, said on July 10.JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts on July 14 that nonbank lenders are already celebrating their competitive advantage."This is great news for hedge funds, private equity, private credit, Apollo, Blackstone," Dimon said, naming two of the largest private equity players. "They're dancing in the streets." (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance is owned by Apollo Global Management.)JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. (Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS) (Elizabeth Frantz / reuters)Many midsize banks that could be part of these new rules are already making adjustments by holding back on any increases in dividends or share buybacks. Several also are selling assets to reduce the risks on their balance sheets or examining a pullback in certain types of lending.Citizens Bank (CFG) has said it will stop originating auto loans. Comerica (CMA) has said it expects to exit the majority of its warehouse lending business by the end of this year."In a perfect world, everything that a bank is doing is profitable," said Scott Siefers, analyst with Piper Sandler. "But if there’s now going to be a higher return requirement, meaning higher capital level, for a given asset, you might need to look more closely at your return."JPMorgan, the nation’s biggest bank, told analysts it might have to raise prices on certain loans."To the extent that we have pricing power and the higher capital requirements mean that we're not generating the right returns for shareholders, we will try to reprice and we'll see how that sticks," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on July 14.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: Fed set to propose new banking capital requirements, 'Basel III endgame'
Text: [Fed officials are set to unveil an overhaul of banking capital requirements, known as the "Basel III endgame," this week. American Banker Staff Writer Kyle Campbell sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to explain the ways in which these guidelines will mitigate risk differently for various forms of credit lending. Campbell describes how these new guidelines will impact certain larger, institutional banks, while examining the exposure regional banks may have to commercial real estate.Video Transcript- All right. On Thursday, just one day after the FOMC's latest interest rate decision, Federal Reserve will unveil a proposal for new bank capital requirements. The proposed rule would also lower the threshold for qualifying banks, meaning smaller institutions will face a new host of demands previously avoided.Fed vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr, outlined a sweeping plan to overhaul bank oversight requirements earlier this month. The proposal, set to come out Thursday, will offer more specifics on just how significant those changes could be.Joining us now with the latest is Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker. Kyle, good to see you here. I talked to Brian Moynihan, CEO of Bank of America, about this. He really took a-- I would say, a hard line view of this. This could really be impactful to the economy. What have you been hearing from sources?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, I mean, that's the big concern, right. Banks have been looking forward to this proposal for a long time now. Since 2017 is when the Basel III, they call it endgame, was first finalized, sort of, internationally, and now we're implementing that.Where this is-- what we're going to see on Thursday is just how that's going to impact the economy because we're going to find out which particular activities are going to be given which sort of risk weights under the new framework. So if, let's say, auto lending comes with a much heavier capital penalty, than a lot of banks are sort of forecasting with their internal models currently. It's going to make that type of financing more expensive, essentially.Story continuesAnd there is a view that as capital overall increases, it's just going to have a broader, sort of, tightening impact on the availability of credit broadly in the economy.- Is it really? Or is it just that their margins are going to get smaller? Or both, right?KYLE CAMPBELL: I think it's probably a bit of both but that's a great question. And certainly, consumer advocates are saying, well, look, the way that capital is raised is it's just hurting the bottom line for executives. You just have to retained earnings and you lose that sort of ROE, return on equity, that is what sort of fuels bank profits.So it's certainly going to result in less profitability, at least for some period of time. And again, how that actually impacts the availability of credit to the average person is going to really, I think-- I don't think it's particularly useful to try to forecast the overall picture, but you can get a good sense of how individual banks are going to be impacted by this once we see the specifics on Thursday.- For those banks, let's say a Wells Fargo, that have been struggling for some time, what does this mean for the struggling banks like a Wells Fargo?KYLE CAMPBELL: Wells Fargo, it'll be interesting. I mean, obviously if-- I mean, they've started to sort of move away from mortgages, which is one area where there's going to be a lot of focus. What happens to mortgages. You know, how does it get treated under the capital rules.I mean-- I think that where it's going to be more impactful than at Wells Fargo-- I mean, certainly they're going to be hit to some degree. But I think it's really going to be most impactful on the sort of mid-size banks, if you will. The ones that were in that sort of 100 billion to 250 billion asset range, that are now going to be facing these capital-- these sort of risk capital requirements for the first time.I think the large banks sort of know how to deal with these sort of requirements. And I don't think that a Wells Fargo is going to be as impacted, on a relative basis, as some of the smaller banks.- Let's turn to another issue that the market's been paying a lot of attention to, and that's commercial real estate and the risks associated with commercial real estate. In these earnings reports that we've gotten from banks, several of them announced steps to anticipate losses. To put aside money for losses, potential losses in commercial real estate.Wells Fargo, for example, boosted its allowance for credit losses. So where are we in that sort of situation?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, that's a great question. And certainly, regulators are very focused on commercial real estate, giving some strong warnings to banks to do things like set aside losses and sort of avoid getting new exposures where you can avoid it.And that actually kind of compounds the issue because a lot of these-- I mean, certainly with offices, we know, the ones that are vacant, not getting people in, and that's sort of a whole issue unto itself. But there are some assets where they're kind of performing relatively well but they're going to need some kind of a recapitalization in order to remain viable and not end up as a foreclosure. And in order to do that, you need banks to sort come to the table.So I think what we're going to be looking for is who's going to move first. Are we going to see some of these sort of big capital equity investors, private equity funds, start to come in and say, hey, we're going to move in in a higher equity basis? Or are we going to see some banks say, hey, actually, we're going to be willing to back some of these recap-type strategies through lending?- Is this a potentially destabilizing event for the banking sector?KYLE CAMPBELL: I wouldn't think so.- I'm trying to compare it to what happened earlier this year.KYLE CAMPBELL: Right. Yeah. I mean, I think you're going to see some serious stress. And I wouldn't be surprised if at specific banks, you see some possible failures. I mean, you don't want to throw that term around too lightly. But yeah, it's possible that some banks could either have to be sold or go through some sort of an M&A activity to sort of right the ship here.I wouldn't expect it to get to a level where we're needing to see serious intervention by the government because they're sort of very well aware of what's going on in real time. But these things can snowball pretty quickly. So yeah, it could be something to watch for sure.- Yeah, most definitely. Kyle, thanks for coming in. Good to see you. Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker, covering some various areas of risks for us.]

Title: PacWest is helping regulators make their case for bolstering US banks
Text: [A regional lender in Beverly Hills may have helped regulators bolster the case they plan to make Thursday to shore up banks across the US.PacWest (PACW), which had been struggling to recover from the downfall of Silicon Valley Bank in March, on Tuesday said it found a rescuer in Banc of California (BANC). The two plan to combine with $400 million in financing from private equity firms Warburg Pincus and Centerbridge.The announcement was a fresh reminder that the turmoil that started in the spring is still not over for the banking industry, which still faces questions about its strength as lenders struggle with high interest rates, rising funding costs, and declining profitability.PacWest stock declined 27% Tuesday and then soared 27% Wednesday.The deal is "a reminder that the stresses on the banking system aren’t all just bad management at one firm," MacroPolicy Perspectives founder Julia Coronado told Yahoo Finance Wednesday. "It is the inverted yield curve, it’s a generational shock in interest rates that banks are having to grapple with ... and that’s a reality that makes it hard for banks to make money."The fresh volatility may come in handy for regulators as the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency try to sell a complex overhaul of new capital standards for banks on Thursday.They argue the changes are needed to make lenders stronger, more resilient, and better prepared for shocks like the crisis of this spring, when the failures of Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, and First Republic triggered deposit withdrawals across the banking world. PacWest, caught up in that panic, sold assets to bolster its liquidity and capital strength.The new capital proposals are expected to face pushback from the banking industry, which argues that lenders are much more resilient than they were during the 2008-09 financial crisis and that higher requirements could restrict lending.Story continuesRead more: How to get a personal loan with bad creditFederal Reserve's vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr. (Andrew Harnik/AP Photo) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr said earlier this month that the Fed would principally raise capital requirements for the largest, most complex banks. The biggest institutions will be asked to hold an additional 2 percentage points of capital — or an additional $2 of capital for every $100 of risk-weighted assets. Capital is the buffer banks have to hold to absorb future losses.He also said regulators would widen the scope of the new rules to institutions with as few as $100 billion in assets, meaning roughly 30 banks would be subject to them. The combined PacWest and Banc of California would be under that cap, based on their combined assets of $36 billion.'Risk weights'These changes are part of the US version of an international accord known as Basel III that was developed following the 2008 crisis by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.The goal of that committee — which was convened by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland — was to set global regulatory capital standards so that banks would have enough in reserve to survive crises. The last version of this accord was agreed to in 2017, but plans to roll it out in the US were delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.A key component of the revised rules will be a series of so-called "risk weights" applied to various assets banks hold. The riskier the assets are, the more capital banks will be required to set aside to absorb any future losses. Those assets can range from Treasuries and mortgages to derivatives and cryptocurrencies.Read more: CDs vs. bonds: Which is right for me?Barr has said that most banks already have enough capital to meet the new standards and estimated that banks would be able to build the required capital through retained earnings in less than two years — even while maintaining their dividends."These changes would increase capital requirements overall, but I want to emphasize that they would principally raise capital requirements for the largest, most complex banks," he said in a speech earlier this month at the Bipartisan Policy Center in Washington.He also made it clear that banks would have time to weigh in with any comments before the proposal is final. "We intend to consider comments carefully and any changes would be implemented with an appropriate phase-in," he said, adding that most banks already have enough capital to meet the new requirements.Betsy Graseck, an equity analyst for Morgan Stanley, said she anticipates the "phase-in" for the largest banks to take three to five years."A later phase in would be a positive for the group as it enables additional capital accretion through earnings generation," Graseck wrote in a Tuesday research note. "An earlier, or shorter, phase in would be a negative."By Graseck’s calculations, JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC) can cover the increased capital requirements from earnings in less than two years’ time. It would take Goldman Sachs (GS) three years and Citigroup (C) four years, she said.'Dancing in the streets'Banks are expected to push back."Further capital requirements on the largest US banks will lead to higher borrowing costs and fewer loans for consumers and businesses — slowing our economy and impacting those on the margin hardest," Kevin Fromer, chief executive of bank lobbying group the Financial Services Forum, said on July 10.JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts on July 14 that nonbank lenders are already celebrating their competitive advantage."This is great news for hedge funds, private equity, private credit, Apollo, Blackstone," Dimon said, naming two of the largest private equity players. "They're dancing in the streets." (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance is owned by Apollo Global Management.)JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. (Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS) (Elizabeth Frantz / reuters)Many midsize banks that could be part of these new rules are already making adjustments by holding back on any increases in dividends or share buybacks. Several also are selling assets to reduce the risks on their balance sheets or examining a pullback in certain types of lending.Citizens Bank (CFG) has said it will stop originating auto loans. Comerica (CMA) has said it expects to exit the majority of its warehouse lending business by the end of this year."In a perfect world, everything that a bank is doing is profitable," said Scott Siefers, analyst with Piper Sandler. "But if there’s now going to be a higher return requirement, meaning higher capital level, for a given asset, you might need to look more closely at your return."JPMorgan, the nation’s biggest bank, told analysts it might have to raise prices on certain loans."To the extent that we have pricing power and the higher capital requirements mean that we're not generating the right returns for shareholders, we will try to reprice and we'll see how that sticks," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on July 14.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Goldman Sachs to run auction of The Telegraph
Text: [telegraph newspaper saleThe investment bank Goldman Sachs has been appointed to run an auction of The Telegraph on behalf of Lloyds Banking Group.Lloyds took ownership last month by sending in receivers. It had been in dispute with the previous owners, the Barclay family, over debts of more than £1bn secured against The Telegraph and The Spectator magazine, which was part of the same group of companies.Goldman will act as lead financial adviser on auctions of The Telegraph and The Spectator, alongside legal advisers from the Magic Circle firm Linklaters, it was announced on Friday. Their appointments were made by the boards of the two parent companies, both of which are chaired by the City veteran Mike McTighe.Lloyds chief executive Charlie Nunn said this week that he was in no rush to sell the titles because both are in robust financial health. However, preparations for the auctions are underway and bidding is expected to begin in September.Despite Mr Nunn’s unhurried posture, senior politicians have publicly warned that the new ownership must be secured as soon as possible. Some have expressed private concerns about a bank owning a Conservatives-supporting publication in the run up to a General Election and the risk of a perception of conflicts of interest.Goldman was appointed ahead of four other investment banks which pitched for the work. Experience in the rigorous running of high-profile sales, knowledge of the media sector and understanding of the potential regulatory and political pitfalls were all factors in the decision. Goldman is known for its political connections, not least in counting the Prime Minister as a former employee.Last time The Telegraph was sold the auction was run by Lazard, which this time has a role advising Lloyds. Its long-standing relationship with DMGT, the owner of The Daily Mail and a potential bidder, is believed to have disqualified it from more direct involvement.The sale of an influential news organisation can hit special regulatory hurdles including tests of whether the new proprietor might be counter to the public interests in media plurality, accurate news and free expression. The risk such rules might pose to some potential bids for The Telegraph is likely to play a significant role in how they are judged, alongside the sum offered.Story continuesEstimates for the value of The Telegraph have varied from as low as £400m to as high as £1bn. The uncertainty is partly caused by the facts that major news organisations very rarely change hands and the media landscape has been transformed by the internet since the Barclay family paid £665m for it in 2004.Last year The Telegraph reported a pre-tax profit of £39m, up 32pc, on turnover of £254m, up 4pc.Broaden your horizons with award-winning British journalism. Title: Goldman Sachs asset management executive Salisbury departs for Sixth Street
Text: [By Lananh Nguyen, Niket Nishant and Manya Saini(Reuters) - Goldman Sachs executive Julian Salisbury will join investment firm Sixth Street as a partner and co-chief investment officer early next year, his incoming firm said, marking yet another high-profile exit from Goldman.Salisbury, who was chief investment officer of asset and wealth management at the Wall Street giant and a member of its management committee, has more than 25 years of investing experience in private and public markets. He steered Goldman's management of $2.7 trillion in assets.Salisbury will reunite with Goldman alums in his new role, including Sixth Street CEO Alan Waxman. The firm manages $65 billion in assets."The prospect of joining their partnership to help drive the next set of investment opportunities became an obvious and compelling proposition," Salisbury wrote in a LinkedIn post.The Goldman veteran joined as an analyst in London in 1998, and later worked in Moscow before moving to New York a decade ago. Salisbury became a partner in 2008 and previously served as global co-head of the asset management unit before it was combined with wealth management under Marc Nachmann last year."Julian is a seamless fit," Waxman said in a statement. "He has distinguished himself time and again as a superstar investor and business builder."A wave of senior personnel has exited from Goldman in recent months. Dina Powell McCormick, head of the bank's sovereign business, recently left to join merchant bank BDT & MSD Partners, led by co-CEO Gregg Lemkau, who previously ran investment banking at Goldman. Katie Koch departed after two decades to become CEO of asset manager TCW Group. Goldman is in a crucial phase as it aims to expand in asset management and undo damage from an ill-fated foray into consumer banking.Goldman's asset management division has promoted 11 partners and hired nine new managing directors focused on investing this year, a company spokeswoman said. Its attrition rate is the lowest in years for investors who are managing portfolios, she said.Story continuesSalisbury has "done a great job putting together all these asset management businesses over the last few years," Nachmann said in an interview. "It’s been great to work with him and I’m excited for him."Goldman's revenue from asset and wealth management slid 4% to $3.05 billion for the second quarter compared with a year earlier, hurt by losses in real estate investments, the bank reported this month. But it also brought in record management fees and assets under supervision.In a memo announcing Salisbury's departure, Goldman CEO David Solomon credited him with unifying five different investment platforms and joining together its traditional and alternative asset management operations.Solomon's plans to sharpen its focus on key businesses such as asset management and trading are gaining traction with the board, two sources close to him told Reuters earlier this month.Salisbury expressed confidence in the bank's leadership to run the division he helped consolidate."Julian operated comfortably in emerging markets, like Russia and China, and took over challenged portfolios in tough times, as in the financial crisis," former Goldman CEO Lloyd Blankfein said. "Always putting the firm first, he was a great partner and I wish him success."(Reporting by Manya Saini and Niket Nishant in Bengaluru, Lananh Nguyen in New York; Editing by Vinay Dwivedi and Matthew Lewis)]

Title: UK's Telegraph and Spectator appoint Goldman Sachs to run sale
Text: [LONDON, July 28 (Reuters) - The boards of the Telegraph newspaper and The Spectator magazine, led by recently appointed chair Mike McTighe, have appointed investment bank Goldman Sachs and law firm Linklaters to advise on their sale, they said in a statement on Friday.Lender Lloyds Banking Group seized control of the centre-right Daily and Sunday Telegraph and the politics-led Spectator last month after their ultimate owners, the Barclay family, failed to repay loans.Lloyds' CEO Charlie Nunn said on Wednesday that the bank would not rush into a sale of the newspapers."At this initial stage, the Boards and their advisers will assess the readiness of the two titles for a sale, including customary vendor due diligence," the parent companies of the titles said.Telegraph Media Group on Tuesday posted a rise in subscriptions and profit in 2022 and said it was on track to meet its target of 1 million subscribers by the end of the year.(Reporting by Paul Sandle)]

Title: Goldman Sachs asset management executive Salisbury departs for Sixth Street
Text: [By Lananh Nguyen, Niket Nishant and Manya Saini(Reuters) - Goldman Sachs executive Julian Salisbury will join investment firm Sixth Street as a partner and co-chief investment officer early next year, his incoming firm said, marking yet another high-profile exit from Goldman.Salisbury, who was chief investment officer of asset and wealth management at the Wall Street giant and a member of its management committee, has more than 25 years of investing experience in private and public markets. He steered Goldman's management of $2.7 trillion in assets.Salisbury will reunite with Goldman alums in his new role, including Sixth Street CEO Alan Waxman. The firm manages $65 billion in assets."The prospect of joining their partnership to help drive the next set of investment opportunities became an obvious and compelling proposition," Salisbury wrote in a LinkedIn post.The Goldman veteran joined as an analyst in London in 1998, and later worked in Moscow before moving to New York a decade ago. Salisbury became a partner in 2008 and previously served as global co-head of the asset management unit before it was combined with wealth management under Marc Nachmann last year."Julian is a seamless fit," Waxman said in a statement. "He has distinguished himself time and again as a superstar investor and business builder."A wave of senior personnel has exited from Goldman in recent months. Dina Powell McCormick, head of the bank's sovereign business, recently left to join merchant bank BDT & MSD Partners, led by co-CEO Gregg Lemkau, who previously ran investment banking at Goldman. Katie Koch departed after two decades to become CEO of asset manager TCW Group. Goldman is in a crucial phase as it aims to expand in asset management and undo damage from an ill-fated foray into consumer banking.Goldman's asset management division has promoted 11 partners and hired nine new managing directors focused on investing this year, a company spokeswoman said. Its attrition rate is the lowest in years for investors who are managing portfolios, she said.Story continuesSalisbury has "done a great job putting together all these asset management businesses over the last few years," Nachmann said in an interview. "Always putting the firm first, he was a great partner and I wish him success."(Reporting by Manya Saini and Niket Nishant in Bengaluru, Lananh Nguyen in New York; Editing by Vinay Dwivedi and Matthew Lewis)]
